questions.stem: A 25-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of a painful, hot, swollen left knee, low back pain with bilateral buttock pain, and left heel pain. There was no history of trauma. He had no fevers or other arthralgias. He had experienced some dysuria several weeks earlier without a noticeable discharge. He was sexually active with other men and engaged in oral and unprotected anal intercourse (insertive and receptive). He had not had any recent screening. On examination, the patient was afebrile with conjunctival injection. There was a rash on his glans penis and his feet, and a large effusion of the left knee. Investigations: Total white cell count 7.3 ×109/L ESR 60 mm/h CRP 20 mg/dL Joint aspiration: Microscopy: no crystals seen white cell count 1000 Gram stain negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Refer to orthopedics for arthroscopic washout
Repeat arthrocentesis with cultures and P16 RNA (16S ribosomal RNA)

questions.explanation: Send urine for gonococcal/chlamydia NAAT Reactive arthritis can have multiple presentations beyond the common findings described in medical textbooks such as conjunctivitis, monoarticular arthritis, and urethritis. This particular patient is a sexually active young male engaging in high-risk sexual behavior, and in this case sexually transmitted infectious etiologies are more likely etiologic agents of reactive arthritis. Clinical findings such as keratoderma blennorrhagicum can be found on the soles of the feet and less commonly on the palms of the hand. It is most commonly due to skin thickening. Circinate balanitis can also occur with a distinct serpiginous annular dermatitis of the glans penis. Empiric therapy for secondary syphilis should not immediately be considered in this case given findings of conjunctivitis, urethritis, and a monoarticular arthritis. Testing for syphilis would not be incorrect in this situation, however. Repeat arthrocentesis testing is not warranted in this case given negative Gram stain and negative culture result from the arthrocentesis fluid. Orthopedic evaluation is not warranted in this situation given the relatively benign appearance of arthrocentesis fluid studies. (Image from Wu IB, Schwartz RA. Reiter’s syndrome: the classic triad and more. J Am Acad Dermatol 59:113-21, 2008.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q9

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presented with an acutely painful left knee and ankle with associated swelling and the inability to bear weight. He had not experienced any fevers or chills. He had not received any recent antibiotics. He was known to have hypertension and atrial fibrillation on warfarin. He described occasional alcohol use. He had recently discontinued his naproxen secondary to gastritis. Investigations: Total white cell count 11,200/mL Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 44 mm/h C-reactive protein 2.9mg/dL Serum uric acid 4.7 mg/dL (normal 3.4–7.0mg/dL) INR 1.8 Left knee aspirate: 10 mL of mildly milky/opaque fluid Synovial fluid microscopy: 740 red blood cells (RBC) 23,000 white blood cells (70% neutrophils) Crystal microscopy pending Cultures pending
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Crystalline arthropathy Basewd on the preliminary results of the synovial fluid cell count and differential, an inflammatory arthritis appears to be present and most likely due to crystalline arthropathy. Effusion due to osteoarthritis is clear, with minimal WBC noted (<2000 white cells) with <25% neutrophils. Given the lack of antecedent antibiotic, we would anticipate turbid synovial fluid and a more robust cell count and differential (septic arthritis is defined as WBC >20,000 cells but can often average ∼50,000 cells and >75% neutrophils) if a septic arthritis was present. While the patient is on anticoagulation on warfarin, we could possibly note reddish synovial fluid if hemarthrosis was present and an elevated RBC relative to WBC. Based on our initial results from the arthrocentesis and patient history of naproxen discontinuation, a crystalline arthropathy would be the most likely diagnosis and would be confirmed by crystal analysis and negative synovial fluid cultures.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q14

questions.question: Practical station: BacT (Aperio digital slides).

parts.text: Blood culture (appeared to show gram-negative bacilli mixed with gram-positive cocci) — which two media are most useful for workup?
Knee aspirate (abundant white blood cells, gram-positive cocci in chains) — describe the smear and give the organism.
CSF (diplococci, poor resolution on the image viewer — gram-positive versus gram-negative cocci) — describe the smear and give the organism.

parts_raw.text: Blood culture (looked like GNB mixed with GPC) - 2 media most useful for workup?
Knee Aspirate (++WBC, GPC in chains) - Describe. What is the organism?
CSF (diplococci, poor resolution on image viewer - ?GPC vs GNC) - Describe. What is the organism?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Blood (sheep) agar — a non-selective medium supporting both organisms and demonstrating hemolysis, with chocolate agar incubated in CO2 for fastidious organisms. (2) MacConkey agar — selective/differential for the gram-negative bacilli and separates them from the gram-positive cocci in a mixed culture; add an anaerobic blood plate if anaerobes are suspected.
b) Abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes with intracellular and extracellular gram-positive cocci in chains — septic arthritis due to a streptococcus, most likely Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) or another beta-hemolytic streptococcus; confirm by catalase (negative), PYR/bacitracin and Lancefield grouping.
c) Numerous leukocytes with intracellular and extracellular gram-negative diplococci with flattened adjacent sides ("coffee-bean"): Neisseria meningitidis. If the diplococci are gram-positive and lancet-shaped in pairs, the organism is Streptococcus pneumoniae — distinguish by oxidase (positive) and growth on Thayer-Martin for N. meningitidis versus optochin susceptibility/bile solubility for S. pneumoniae; repeat/counterstain the smear if resolution is inadequate.

questions.question: A 14-month-old presents with septic arthritis and osteomyelitis.

parts.text: When will you see x-ray changes?
What are the two most common x-ray changes?
What is the most common bug and the necessary treatment?
What is the duration of treatment?

parts_raw.text: When will you see X-ray changes?
What are the 2 most common X-ray changes?
Most common bug and necessary treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Radiographs are insensitive early; bony abnormality is usually seen 10 to 14 days after onset (CPS: 7-21 days); soft tissue swelling may appear within the first few days.
b) (1) Periosteal elevation with periosteal new bone formation. (2) Metaphyseal lytic/lucent destructive lesions (sclerosis follows after about a month).
c) Staphylococcus aureus. Treat methicillin-susceptible disease with intravenous cefazolin or nafcillin/oxacillin, stepping down to oral cephalexin once afebrile and improving; use vancomycin if MRSA is suspected or prevalent. Purulent joint involvement also requires surgical drainage/arthrotomy.
d) Minimum 3 weeks of total therapy for uncomplicated disease (Mandell: typical pediatric duration 3 weeks), commonly 3-4 weeks, and longer (4-6 weeks) for complicated infection or hip septic arthritis.
questions.beyond_mandell: CPS 2018 osteoarticular infection statement supplies the 7-21 day radiographic window and the 3-4 week (up to 4-6 week) duration ranges.

cohort_answer.text: X-ray changes: soft tissue swelling at 3 days; lytic lesions, periosteal elevation, periosteal new bone formation at 10-20 days (7-21 days per CPS); sclerosis of bone after a month. Most common changes: periosteal reaction (new bone formation) and periosteal elevation (suggests abscess). Bug/treatment: Staph aureus (MSSA or MRSA depending on local epidemiology), Cloxacillin or Cefazolin for MSSA, Vancomycin for MRSA. Duration: 3-6 weeks (septic arthritis 3 weeks minimum, OM 4-6 weeks); uncomplicated AO/SA generally 3-4 weeks (4-6 weeks for hip SA).

questions.question: A 2-year-old child presents with a few days of favouring the left leg due to right knee pain. Ultrasound is normal, but MRI shows bone marrow edema of the distal femur.
questions.question_raw: A 2-year old child presents with a few day history of favouring their left leg due to pain on the right knee. The child undergoes ultrasound showing no abnormality but an MRI shows bone marrow edema of the distal femur.

parts.text: Blood cultures grow a gram-negative coccobacillus; what is the MOST likely organism?
What non-osteoarticular infection is this organism most likely to cause?

parts_raw.text: The blood cultures result in a gram-negative coccobacilli, what is the MOST likely organism?
What NON-osteoarticular infection is this organism above most likely to cause?

questions.model_answer:
a) Osteomyelitis of the distal femur (acute osteoarticular infection).
b) Kingella kingae, the most common cause of osteoarticular infection in previously healthy children younger than 4 years, presenting subtly with often-normal acute-phase reactants.
c) Endocarditis (Kingella is the K of the HACEK group and, unlike its osteoarticular disease, can cause endocarditis at all ages, on native or prosthetic valves).

questions.question: A 26-year-old man with sepsis and a swollen, painful knee has a blood culture positive for gram-negative diplococci (no sexual history given).
questions.question_raw: 26-year-old guy with sepsis and swollen painful knee, has a blood culture positive for gram negative diplococci (doesn't mention sexual history).

parts.text: What is the most likely organism (genus/species)?
What three other microbiologic tests should you order?
What are three host factors for dissemination?

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely organism (genus/species)
What three other microbiologic tests should you order
What are 3 host factors for dissemination?

questions.model_answer: a) Neisseria gonorrhoeae. b) (1) HIV testing (4th-generation Ag/Ab); (2) syphilis serology; (3) C. trachomatis NAAT plus mucosal N. gonorrhoeae testing (urethra, rectum, pharynx) and NAAT/culture of synovial fluid - all people with a new STI should be screened for coexisting STIs. c) (1) Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C8); (2) female sex and menstruation (symptoms often begin within 7 days of menses); (3) pharyngeal gonococcal infection (pregnancy is also cited).

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Other tests: HIV p24 Ag/Ab; Syphilis screen (EIA, RPR, TPPA); Urine NAAT for C. trachomatis. Host factors for dissemination: Recent menstruation; Pregnancy or the immediate postpartum state; Congenital or acquired complement deficiencies (C5-C8); Eculizumab; SLE (conflicting reports)
